meta.blurb: Two hard-working friends in ancient Babylon cannot understand why their purses are always empty. They go to Arkad, the richest man in the city, and learn how he began with nothing but a habit and some patience.
meta.bible: Babylon: the great walled city of the story, with its market, its river and its clay tablets. Bansir: a chariot-maker, proud of his skill, always short of silver. Kobbi: his friend, a musician who plays his lute at feasts. Arkad: the richest man in Babylon, once a poor scribe, calm and kind; he tells the story. Algamish: the money-lender who hired young Arkad to copy tablets and taught him to keep one part in ten. Dabasir: a former slave who owed many debts and paid every one; his story is on clay tablets from Nippur. Nippur: a city far from Babylon, where the tablets came from. Mathon: a money-lender who helped Dabasir plan his repayments and spoke about borrowing. Hadan: an invented potter, the lucky man who found a purse of silver and lost it again. Invented, unnamed minor figures: a brickmaker, a friend who traded in jewels, camel traders, a sheep farmer, a smiling stranger and two wise men. Money is silver and gold, pieces of silver, shekels and clay tablets; keep ancient detail simple and do not invent historical facts. The seven cures for a lean purse: keep one part in ten of all you earn; control your spending; make your gold work by lending it wisely; guard it against loss and ask the wise; make your home a good investment; plan an income for later; increase your own ability to earn. The five laws of gold are in the story. Voice: calm, wise and slow, like an elder speaking at the end of the day. This is a story about habits and patience, never a promise of riches and never advice for the reader's own money.

B1B2: Bansir and Kobbi, two old friends, sat against the great wall of Babylon as the evening sun went down. Both of them were tired and dusty after a long day of work.
Bansir took out his old leather purse and turned it over, but nothing fell out. “I make good chariots,” he said, “yet I have never had enough silver.”
Kobbi sighed and rested his lute on his knee, for he knew the same story well. “I play at every feast in the city,” he said, “but the coins slip through my fingers like water.”
A rich merchant rolled past them in a chariot trimmed with gold, and his servants hurried along behind him. “Why does gold come so easily to some men,” Bansir asked, “and so hard to the rest of us?”
Kobbi stopped and thought, and then he smiled for the first time that day. Everyone said that Arkad was the richest man in Babylon, and some people said he had begun with very little.
Bansir hesitated, afraid that a rich man would laugh at two poor workers. In the end, however, his wish to understand was stronger than his pride, and the friends shook hands.
The next morning the friends put on their cleanest robes and walked through the busy streets. Bakers, water carriers and traders called out to them, but they kept their eyes on the road ahead.
Arkad's house was large, but it was not loud or proud, and a garden of palm trees grew behind its gate. A servant listened to their request and then led them inside to wait.
Arkad was a calm, grey-haired man with kind eyes, and he asked them to sit. Bansir put to him the question they had carried for so long: why do men who work hard so often stay poor?
“I was once as poor as you,” said Arkad, “a young scribe who pressed words into wet clay.” He wrote from morning to night for very little silver and saw no road to anything better.
One day a money-lender named Algamish hired Arkad to copy a long law onto clay tablets. The work was hard and slow, but Arkad was glad of the extra silver.
When the work was done, Algamish asked what became of the silver the young man earned. “I spend it all on food, rent and a few small pleasures,” Arkad said, “and soon it is gone.”
“A part of all you earn is yours to keep,” said Algamish. “Set aside one part in every ten before you spend anything else, for that is where a full purse begins.”
At first Arkad doubted that he could live on nine parts when ten had never been enough. Even so, he dropped the first piece of silver into a small clay jar and promised to try for a year.

To his surprise, Arkad found that nine parts of his pay bought almost as much food and comfort as ten had done. After a few months the little jar began to feel heavy in his hands, and he felt proud of it.
“This is the first cure for a lean purse,” Arkad told his visitors. “Start your purse to fattening: keep one part in ten of all you earn, and do not break the habit.”

“The second cure is to control your spending,” said Arkad, and he leaned forward to make sure they were listening. “Not every want is a need, and a man who counts his wants will find that many of them fade away.”

Kobbi thought about last month and laughed with embarrassment, for he could not remember where half his silver went. Arkad advised them both to write down every purchase for a month, because numbers do not flatter a man.

After a year, Algamish asked what Arkad had done with his savings, and he frowned to hear they sat in a jar. “Silver in a jar does no work,” he said, “so lend it carefully, and let it earn a little for you.”
Arkad lent a small part of his savings to a brickmaker who needed a new kiln for his work. At year's end the man returned every piece and a little more, and Arkad saw his silver had worked.

The fourth cure, Arkad said, is to guard gold against loss, and he had learned it the hard way. He lent much of his savings to a friend who wished to trade in jewels, though neither of them knew stones.
After that, Arkad asked wise men who knew each trade before he lent any silver. He learned that a safe loan has a clear purpose and a borrower who can repay it, and he never forgot it.
“The fifth cure is to make your home a good investment,” Arkad said. “Rent is silver that is gone for ever, but a home that is paid for belongs to its owner.”
“The sixth cure is to plan for your old age and for your family,” Arkad said. “The day will come when your hands are too weak to work, and a wise man prepares for it long before.”
“The seventh cure is to increase your own ability to earn,” said Arkad. “A man who studies his trade and takes pride in his work becomes worth more to those who need him.”

A servant brought bread, figs and cool water, and the three men ate as the shadows grew longer. “None of these cures works in a day,” Arkad said, “and a purse grows only through slow, patient habits.”
“Now I will tell you the five laws of gold,” said Arkad. “The first law is this: gold comes gladly to the man who keeps at least one part in ten.”
“The second law is that gold works hard for a wise owner who finds it good work to do,” Arkad said. “In careful hands even a little silver can work well, but it works slowly,” he added.

“The third law is that gold stays with the careful owner who asks the advice of wise men,” Arkad said. “Those who ask first lose less, because the wise have already seen the mistakes others are about to make.”
“The fourth law is that gold slips away from the man who puts it into things he does not understand,” said Arkad. “My friend and his jewels taught me this, and I have not forgotten it since.”

“The fifth law is that gold flees from the man who asks impossible gains of it,” Arkad said. “A trickster's promise of sudden wealth is usually a trap, and the man who follows it often loses what he has.”
Next Arkad spoke of luck, and he told of a potter named Hadan who found a purse of silver on the road. Hadan was delighted, for he had never held so much silver at one time.
Hadan bought fine clothes and gave great feasts, and within a season the silver was gone. He was a poor potter again, because luck had brought him silver but not the habits to keep it.
Then Arkad sent a servant for a wooden chest full of clay tablets from the city of Nippur. They had been written, he explained, by a man named Dabasir, who had once been a slave.
Dabasir had been a slave, and when he was finally free he found himself owing money to many people. He owned very little, he was ashamed, and he did not know how he would ever pay them back.

Dabasir was afraid of his creditors, but he went to Mathon the money-lender and asked what he should do. Mathon did not laugh at him, and he said that the first step was always to look at the whole truth.

Mathon showed him how to divide his earnings: enough to live on, and the rest in shares for each creditor. “Pay a little to everyone,” Mathon said, “and no one will have a reason to stop trusting you.”

While they talked, Mathon also taught him a hard lesson about borrowing, which he said many young men learn too late. “Borrow only what you can repay,” he said, “and never borrow for pleasures that are soon forgotten.”
Dabasir went to every creditor, told them the plain truth and showed them his plan. They agreed to wait, and after some years he paid the last piece of silver and owed nothing at all.

Arkad also lent small amounts to camel traders, who needed silver to buy animals before each long journey. He chose carefully, because a caravan can fail on the road, and he never put all his silver into one loan.
Arkad also lent to a sheep farmer who needed to buy more sheep for his flock. The farmer repaid the loan from the wool and lambs he sold, and Arkad saw that slow, honest work paid both sides.

Years later, when Arkad's savings had grown, a stranger in a bright robe came to his door with a wonderful plan. He promised to double Arkad's silver in one month, and he spoke so smoothly that even a careful man might have listened.

Arkad took the plan to two wise men he trusted, and both of them warned him to stay away. He refused the stranger, and he later heard that several people who had trusted the man had lost most of their savings.
At last Arkad told them that gold is a tool, not the whole of life, and it serves best by easing worry. “Keep these habits for years, not for days,” he said, “and let time do its quiet work.”
Bansir and Kobbi thanked Arkad warmly and walked home through the quiet streets of Babylon. For a long while neither spoke, but they both felt lighter than they had felt in years.
The next evening, each man counted his earnings and set aside one part in every ten in a clay jar. “It is not much,” said Kobbi, “but it is more than we have ever kept before.”

The first months were not easy, because many things in the market seemed to call out to them. Kobbi wanted a bright new cloak and Bansir wanted better tools, but each time they remembered the jar, and they waited.

After a year their jars had grown heavy, and the friends returned to Arkad to ask how to lend a little wisely. He asked careful questions, as wise men had asked him, and told them to start small and stay near what they knew.
Little by little the years went by, and the two purses grew fatter. Bansir moved into a bigger workshop with an apprentice, and Kobbi played at feasts with a lighter heart.

One evening the two friends sat again by the great wall, where they had once asked their sad question. A young man stopped to hear about Arkad, and Bansir said, “Keep one part in ten, and be patient.”
C1C2: The sun sank slowly behind the great wall of Babylon, turning its bricks the colour of honey, and the noise of the market began to fade. Bansir the chariot-maker and Kobbi the musician, friends since boyhood, sat in its shadow with the heavy tiredness of men who had worked since dawn. Neither of them spoke for a long while, for the day had asked much of them and given very little back.

Bansir pulled out his worn leather purse, turned it upside down, and let the wind carry off the dust that was all it held. “I build the finest chariots in the city, and the best wheels,” he said bitterly, “and still my purse is as light as a feather.” His hands, scarred by years of timber and bronze, lay open on his knees as though they too were asking a question.

Kobbi, who had been listening with his lute across his lap, gave a short laugh that held no joy. “I play at every wedding and every feast in Babylon, and men praise my music,” he said, “yet by the end of each month the praise is all I have left.” The two friends looked at each other, and each saw his own trouble reflected in the other's face.

Along the road rolled a chariot trimmed with gold, pulled by two fine horses and followed by servants who ran to keep pace with their master. Bansir watched it pass with the quiet envy of a craftsman who knew exactly what such a vehicle cost to build. At last he asked, “What is it that the gods bestow on some men and withhold from honest workers who toil as hard as we do?”

Kobbi sat up suddenly as a thought struck him, and a slow smile spread across his weathered face. “Arkad is called the richest man in all Babylon,” he said, “and men whisper that he began with no more than we have today.” “If any man living can explain the secret of gold, it is he, and I have heard that he listens kindly to an honest question.”

Bansir hesitated, for it is a hard thing for a proud man to knock at a rich man's door and admit that his own purse is empty. Yet the question had troubled him for years, and he knew that another year of silence would answer nothing. They clasped hands as the first stars appeared above the wall and agreed to go at first light.

At dawn they set out through streets already loud with bakers, water carriers and merchants shouting the prices of dates and wool. Each man had put on his cleanest robe, and each carried, beneath his pride, a small hope that he was too embarrassed to name. By the time the sun stood above the walls, they had reached the quiet, tree-lined quarter where the wealthy of Babylon lived.

The house of Arkad was large and handsome, yet it showed none of the glitter they had expected, and behind its gate lay a quiet garden shaded by palm trees. A servant heard their request, studied their dusty sandals with polite curiosity, and left them to wait in the cool shade. Before long he returned, bowed, and said that his master would receive them at once in the shade of the inner courtyard.

Arkad proved to be a calm man with silver hair and eyes that seemed to weigh each word before it was spoken. He asked them to sit, listened to their story without once interrupting, and nodded as Bansir finally put the question into words. “Why,” said Bansir, “do men who work as hard as we do so often remain poor while others, who seem to work no harder, grow rich?”

“I was once as poor as you are,” said Arkad, settling back in his seat, “a young scribe in the city, pressing the language of other men into wet tablets of clay.” From dawn until the lamps were lit he copied their contracts, accounts and laws, and he was paid so little that he could scarcely call a piece of silver his own. In those days, he told them, he had believed that poverty was simply the fate of men who earned their bread with their hands or their reeds.

Among the men for whom Arkad wrote was Algamish, a money-lender known throughout Babylon for his shrewd mind and his heavy purse. He hired the young scribe to copy a long law onto clay tablets, paying him a small sum at the end of each day. Arkad, though weary, was glad of the work, and he little guessed how much it would change the rest of his life.

When the last tablet was finished, Algamish put down his reed and asked the scribe what became of the silver he earned. “I spend all of it,” Arkad admitted, “on food, rent and the small pleasures that make a hard life bearable, and by the week's end nothing is left.” Algamish nodded slowly, as though the answer were one he had heard a hundred times from men who worked hard and had nothing to show for it.

“A part of all you earn is yours to keep,” said Algamish, leaning forward until the lamplight caught the lines of his face. “Set aside one part in every ten the moment it reaches your hand, before the baker, the landlord or your own wishes can claim it, and never touch it for pleasure.” He added that this single habit, kept faithfully, was the seed from which every purse of any size had first begun to grow.

Arkad could not hide his doubt, for he had always found ten parts too few and could not see how nine would be enough. Yet he trusted the money-lender's judgment more than his own habits, and that evening he dropped a piece of silver into a small clay jar and set it on a high shelf. He promised himself that he would keep the habit for a full year before he judged whether it was wise.

To his astonishment, Arkad discovered that nine parts of his earnings kept him almost as well fed and clothed as ten had done, for the tenth had always melted away on small wants. Month by month the little jar grew heavier, and with its weight came a feeling he had not known before: the quiet pride of a man who owned something. It was a small thing, he knew, but it was the first thing that belonged to him alone.

“Here is the first cure for a lean purse,” Arkad told them, and he held up a small clay jar as plain as any in the market. “Start your purse to fattening: keep one part in ten of everything you earn, and let no season of need or temptation break the habit.” He did not promise that it would make them rich, only that every fuller purse had once begun in the same way.

“The second cure is to control your spending,” said Arkad, drawing a line down the middle of a clay tablet. “On one side I wrote what a man truly needs, on the other what he merely wishes for, and I found that the second column was always longer, and always more expensive.” “A wise man does not strike out every wish,” he added, “but he lets each one wait until the purse can bear it.”

Kobbi thought of the wine he had shared with strangers, the sandals he had not truly needed and the gifts he had given merely to be liked, and he laughed ruefully. Arkad said that there was no shame in it, for most men are blind to their small spendings until they see them laid out in a row. He urged them to mark every purchase on clay for one month, because, as he put it, a tablet does not flatter anyone.

After a year Algamish asked what Arkad had done with his savings, and he frowned when he learned that they lay untouched in a jar. “Silver that sleeps earns nothing,” he said, “and a man who wants his gold to multiply must lend it, carefully and in small amounts, to people who can put it to honest use.” He explained that a fair payment for such a loan was the gold's way of working while its owner slept.

Arkad lent a small part of his savings to a brickmaker who needed a new kiln, having first walked to the man's yard to see that his work was sound. When the year ended, the brickmaker returned every piece of silver together with a fair payment for its use, and not a day late. Arkad held the extra pieces in his palm and understood, for the first time, that his silver could work as faithfully as he did.

The fourth cure, Arkad said, is to guard your gold against loss, and he had learned it in the most painful way. In his early eagerness he lent a large part of his savings to a friend who meant to trade in jewels, although neither of them could tell a true stone from a worthless one. The friend was honest enough but ignorant of his trade, and the silver, once spent, was never seen by Arkad again.

From then on he went first to those who understood each trade, the merchants, the farmers and the money-lenders, and he asked them what could go wrong before he risked a single piece. He learned that a safe loan has a clear purpose, a borrower of good character and some security, and that the pleasure of a large promise is no protection at all. Guarding his gold, he came to see, was less about fear than about the humility to ask for advice.

“The fifth cure is to make your home a profitable investment,” said Arkad, and he gestured at the roof and courtyard around them. “Every month a man pays rent, that silver is gone for ever, but the man who pays towards a home of his own builds something his family may keep.” He added that a home of one's own brings shelter and quiet pride, and that a family which owns its roof is less afraid of the future.

“The sixth cure is to provide for the future,” said Arkad, nodding towards an old porter who rested in the shade beyond the wall. “Strong hands and young eyes will not last for ever, and a man should set aside the means to care for his old age and his family while he is still able.” He did not say how much was enough, only that the work of providing for later is best begun while a man is strong.

“The seventh cure,” said Arkad, turning to Bansir, “is to increase your own ability to earn, for a man who learns more of his craft is a better friend to his own purse.” “A chariot-maker who studies the weight of every wheel and the grain of every plank,” he went on, “will in time be sought out by those who value the difference.” Bansir, who had always been proud of his skill, found himself looking at his own scarred hands with new attention.

A servant brought bread, figs and cool water, and the three men ate in silence for a time while the shadows of the palms lengthened across the courtyard. “None of these seven cures works in a day,” Arkad said at last, “for the habits of years cannot be undone by the enthusiasm of an afternoon.” “A purse fattens as a tree grows,” he went on, “by small gains that no one notices, and by seasons that have no wish to hurry.”

As the afternoon grew golden, Arkad said that he would now give them the five laws of gold, which he had learned from Algamish and tested for many years. The first, he said, is that gold comes gladly and in steady amounts to the man who keeps at least one part in ten of all his earnings. He stressed that this was not magic but plain arithmetic, for a sum that is put aside every day becomes larger, however slowly, while a sum never put aside remains nothing.

“The second law,” said Arkad, weighing a small bag of silver in his palm, “is that gold labours diligently for the wise owner who finds it profitable employment, and that it does so patiently.” He compared such gold to a faithful servant, willing to work day and night, but only for a master who knows where to send it. Left idle or sent into the hands of the careless, he warned, it will wander off and bring its owner nothing but regret.

“The third law,” Arkad continued, “is that gold clings to the careful owner who invests it under the advice of wise men.” “The inexperienced man trusts his own hopes,” he said, “and the wise man trusts those who have walked the road before him, and who can tell him which bridges are sound.” “It costs a little pride to ask, but pride is a poor shield when a purse is at risk.”

“The fourth law,” said Arkad, “is that gold slips away from the man who puts it into ventures he does not understand.” He reminded them of his friend and the jewels, and said that a glittering stone, like a glittering promise, is no proof of worth. A man should keep his gold within the limits of what he knows, he added, and ask for help at the edge of his own understanding.

“The fifth law,” Arkad said, raising a finger as the servants lit the lamps, “is that gold flees from the man who demands impossible gains from it, or who follows the advice of tricksters.” He had seen many men ruined by the whisper of a sudden fortune, he said, and he warned the two friends that such offers always sound sweetest to those who are tired of being poor. The five laws, he concluded, were not complicated, but they were easy to forget, which was why he repeated them to himself each morning.

Kobbi asked about luck, for he had often envied the men to whom good fortune seemed to come without the slightest effort. Arkad answered with the story of a potter named Hadan, who one dusty morning found a heavy purse of silver lying beside the road. Never in all his years at the wheel had he held so much at one time, and he stood in the road for a long moment, unable to believe his luck.

Hadan bought rich robes and a donkey cart, gave feasts for friends who had never greeted him before, and trusted that the gods, having been so generous once, would be generous again. Within a single season the purse was empty and the friends were gone, and the potter returned to his wheel as poor as before, with nothing to show for his good fortune. “Luck had come to him by chance,” said Arkad, “and it left him by chance, for he had no habit that could hold it.”

As the lamps burned brighter, Arkad sent a servant for a wooden chest, and from it he lifted baked clay tablets with worn edges and careful rows of marks. They came from the city of Nippur, he told his guests, and had been written by a man named Dabasir, who had once been a slave. Arkad kept them, he said, because they told of a man who owed much and still found his way.

Dabasir had spent years as a slave, and when his freedom came he found that he had also gathered debts, owing small sums to the baker, the cloth-seller, the landlord and many more. He owned almost nothing, he felt ashamed to walk the streets where his creditors lived, and he could not imagine how a man in his position would ever be free of them. Like many people who owe much, he was tempted to hide from the problem rather than face it.

At last Dabasir went to Mathon, a money-lender who dealt with many debtors, and asked what a man in his place should do. Mathon did not laugh at him or scold him, and he said only that fear grows in the dark and that the first step was to write down every debt, every name and every sum. It was, Dabasir later wrote, the first time he had felt that his trouble might have an end.

Mathon showed him a simple method: keep enough to live on, and divide the rest among his creditors in shares that matched what he owed to each. “A small payment from an honest man is worth more to a creditor than a large promise from a man who hides,” said Mathon, “because trust grows with every payment.” Dabasir went home that night and set out small piles of silver in a row, one for each name on his list.

Mathon spoke next of borrowing, which he said was a useful tool in careful hands and a heavy chain in careless ones. “Borrow only what you can see a clear way to repay,” he said, “and be careful with loans for pleasure, because the pleasure fades in a night while the debt stays for years.” He added that he would lend gladly to a man with a trade and a plan, but never to one who borrowed to hide an empty purse.

One by one Dabasir visited his creditors, told them the plain truth and laid his plan before them, and he found that many were willing to wait for an honest man. He kept every promise he made, paying on the day he had named and never hiding behind an excuse, and the years of small payments slowly lightened the weight he carried. At last he gave the final piece of silver to the baker, and for the first time since his freedom he owed nothing to anyone.

Arkad went on to tell how he lent small sums to camel traders, who needed silver to buy their animals before each long journey across the desert. He walked among the camels himself, questioned the men who had travelled with each trader, and never put all his silver into one caravan. Where he judged the man honest and the plan sound, however, the loans came back with a fair payment, and his silver slowly learned to work in many places at once.

With a sheep farmer from the river plains, Arkad made a different kind of bargain, lending him silver to buy more animals for his flock in the spring. The farmer repaid the loan, little by little, from the wool and the lambs he sold, and in the process Arkad saw that his gold, like the flock, grew only by patience and by seasons. A bad winter could have thinned the flock and delayed the repayment, he admitted, which was why he had never lent more to one farmer than he could afford to wait for.

Years later, when Arkad's silver had grown enough to be noticed, a stranger in a bright robe came to his door with a scheme so splendid that he could barely keep still. He promised to double Arkad's silver within a single month, to ask only a small share for himself, and to smile warmly whenever a doubt was raised. Arkad, who had learned at some cost to listen first and trust afterwards, asked the stranger a few plain questions and found that the man could not answer a single one.

Arkad carried the plan to two wise men who knew trade, and both warned him that a promise of great gain in a short time is usually paid for by the one who believes it. He refused the offer politely, and some months later he heard that several of those who had trusted the stranger had lost most of what they owned. “Gold asks for patience,” Arkad said to his visitors, “and any man who promises to take the patience out of it is selling something other than gold.”

As the day closed, Arkad walked with them to the garden gate and spoke quietly of what gold is for. It is a tool and a servant, he said, never the whole of a good life, and its best gift is the calm of a man who no longer lies awake at night. “Keep these habits for years and not for days,” he told them, laying a hand on Bansir's shoulder, “and be content to let time do its slow and honest work.”

Bansir and Kobbi thanked Arkad with more feeling than either could put into words, and then they walked home together through streets that had grown quiet beneath a sky full of stars. For a long time neither man spoke, since each was turning over what he had heard, as a craftsman turns a tool he has just been taught to use. Then Kobbi laughed softly, for the answer to the question that had weighed on them for years had been so simple to say and so hard to practise.

That very evening each of them counted his day's earnings and set aside one part in every ten in a plain clay jar, Bansir in his workshop and Kobbi in his rented room. “It is not much,” Kobbi said, weighing the little pile in his palm, “but it is more than I have kept in all my years of playing.” Bansir only nodded, for he had learned from Arkad not to despise a small beginning, and not to mistake it for the end.

The first months were hard, for the market seemed to have grown louder and its goods brighter than ever before, and each friend felt the pull of a hundred small wants. Kobbi longed for a cloak the colour of the evening sky and Bansir for a set of fine new tools, but when they met they reminded one another of the jars, and the wish passed. Neither complained aloud, though both discovered how much of their old spending had been habit rather than need.

When a year had passed, their jars had grown noticeably heavier, and the friends returned to Arkad's garden to ask how they might put a little of that silver to work. He did not give them a plan so much as a method, asking who the borrower was, what he meant to do, how he would repay and what would be lost if he could not. Then he urged them to begin with small sums, to stay close to the trades they understood and to be in no hurry, which he said was the hardest of all.

The years went quietly by, and, as Arkad had said, the change came not in a day but in the sum of many ordinary ones. Bansir's jar had grown into a modest purse, lent here and there with care, and it let him move into a larger workshop where an apprentice learned at his side. Kobbi, for his part, played at feasts without the old anxious hurry for the coins, and he found that his music was better for it.

Years after that first visit, the two friends sat again beneath the great wall of Babylon at the close of day, with purses that no longer felt light enough to blow away. A young man passing by, weary from a day of labour and heavy with the same old question, stopped to listen as they told him of Arkad and the seven cures. When they had finished, Bansir smiled and said only that the secret was less a secret than a habit, and that the best day to begin it was a day like any other.
